items.text: The scenario scaffold is at 99/100 completeness with 470+ tests and 97% Go API coverage, but the current implementation covers only the foundational CRUD layer: schemes, information items, thoughts, edges, export, and LLM suggestion stubs. Several core differentiating features from the spec are not yet implemented: (1) voice capture with Whisper transcription, (2) agent-manager chat integration, (3) offline-first with IndexedDB/service worker sync, (4) canvas virtualization with spatial indexing, (5) LLM-powered ghost node generation with actual Ollama/OpenRouter calls, and (6) the export-to-scenario flow. The plan needs to be updated to reflect what's been built and define phased delivery of the remaining features.

items.context: Six major features remain unbuilt. They have different dependency chains and complexity levels. Building them all at once would be unwieldy. Recommend Phase A (voice + canvas virtualization — core capture UX), Phase B (ghost nodes + offline sync — intelligence + resilience), Phase C (agent chat + export flow — integration features). This front-loads the features that define the core user experience.

options.label: Phase A → B → C as described (capture UX first)
options.rationale: Voice capture and canvas performance are the core differentiators. Getting these right first validates the UX thesis before investing in integrations.

options.label: Voice + offline first, then canvas + ghost nodes, then integrations
options.rationale: Offline-first is architecturally foundational — adding it later means retrofitting IndexedDB/sync into every feature. Doing it early avoids rework.

options.label: All features in parallel as separate work items
options.rationale: Maximum parallelism — each feature is independent enough for separate agents. Higher coordination cost but faster wall-clock time.

options.label: Other
options.rationale: Provide your own phasing strategy

items.topic: Canvas library selection for virtualization and touch handling
items.context: The current CanvasView is a basic div-based implementation with manual drag/pan/zoom handlers. The spec calls for virtualized rendering with spatial indexing to handle 200+ items on mobile. This is a significant architectural upgrade. The plan mentions react-flow but there are alternatives with different tradeoffs for a mobile-first spatial canvas.

options.label: React Flow (reactflow.dev)
options.rationale: Mature, well-documented, built-in viewport culling and minimap. Primarily designed for node-graph UIs (flowcharts). May feel over-structured for a freeform spatial canvas — nodes are connected, not freely floating. Touch support exists but is secondary to desktop.

options.label: Custom canvas with quadtree spatial index
options.rationale: Full control over touch interactions and mobile UX. More work but exactly fits the freeform spatial layout use case. No library overhead or fighting library opinions. Use a quadtree library (e.g., d3-quadtree) for viewport culling.

options.label: Konva.js / react-konva (HTML5 Canvas)
options.rationale: GPU-accelerated 2D rendering via HTML5 Canvas element. Excellent performance with many items. Built-in touch support. Downside: canvas-rendered content isn't DOM — harder to style, no native text input, accessibility challenges.

options.label: Excalidraw-based (fork or embed)
options.rationale: Already solves freeform spatial canvas with touch, collaboration, and infinite canvas. Rich feature set but heavy dependency and may be hard to customize for the specific thought-capture UX.

options.label: Other
options.rationale: Provide your own approach

items.topic: Voice capture: browser MediaRecorder vs dedicated recording library
items.context: The voice capture feature needs to record audio, stream it to Whisper for real-time transcription, and place the result on the canvas. The plan specifies mirroring web-console's Whisper integration (WebSocket streaming + HTTP batch). The recording side has two main approaches.

options.label: Browser MediaRecorder API directly
options.rationale: No additional dependency. Well-supported across browsers. Outputs WebM/Opus by default (needs ffmpeg transcoding to WAV for Whisper). Straightforward to stream chunks via WebSocket. Mirrors what web-console likely does.

options.label: RecordRTC or similar recording library
options.rationale: Handles cross-browser codec differences, provides WAV output directly (no server-side transcoding), supports pause/resume. Adds ~50KB dependency but reduces backend complexity.

options.label: Other
options.rationale: Provide your own approach

items.topic: Offline sync: when to implement the IndexedDB/service worker layer
items.context: The spec requires offline-first operation. Currently, all data goes directly to PostgreSQL via the API with no local persistence. Adding offline support is architecturally invasive — it affects every data mutation path (write local first, sync in background). Retrofitting it later means touching every existing feature. However, for a Vrooli server deployment (always-on local server), offline is less critical than for a mobile PWA on the go.

options.label: Implement offline layer before new features
options.rationale: Every new feature (voice, agent chat, ghost nodes) will need to work offline. Building the sync layer first means new features automatically get offline support. Avoids costly retrofit.

options.label: Defer offline to a dedicated phase after core features
options.rationale: The primary deployment is a local Vrooli server where the API is always reachable. Offline matters most for future mobile PWA use. Build core features first against the API, then add the offline layer as a dedicated phase that wraps all mutations.

options.label: Implement a thin offline queue now, full sync later
options.rationale: Add a simple mutation queue (IndexedDB write-through) that captures failed API calls and retries on reconnect. Not full offline-first, but handles intermittent connectivity. Low effort now, full implementation later.

options.label: Other
options.rationale: Provide your own approach

items.topic: Agent chat integration: embedded panel vs agent-manager API calls
items.context: The spec calls for an agent-manager-powered chat panel with read/write access to the scheme. Agent-manager is a separate Vrooli scenario. The integration approach affects how tightly coupled these scenarios become.

options.label: Embedded iframe from agent-manager UI
options.rationale: Minimal coupling — agent-manager provides a chat widget URL, stream-of-consciousness-analyzer embeds it with scheme context via postMessage. Agent-manager handles all chat UX. Downsides: iframe styling constraints, limited control over quick-action buttons.

options.label: Direct API calls to agent-manager's chat endpoint
options.rationale: Build a custom chat UI in stream-of-consciousness-analyzer that calls agent-manager's API for completions. Full control over UX and quick-action buttons. Tighter coupling but better integration. Agent gets scheme context via API read calls.

options.label: Shared chat component library
options.rationale: Extract a reusable chat component from agent-manager that both scenarios can use. Best long-term reusability but highest initial effort. Requires coordinating with agent-manager's codebase.

options.label: Other
options.rationale: Provide your own approach

items.text: The existing SuggestionService has the provider selection infrastructure (Ollama primary, OpenRouter fallback) and database schema for suggestions, but the actual LLM call to generate suggestions is not yet implemented — GenerateSuggestions returns stub data. The throttling, batching, and ghost node rendering in the graph view also need to be built. This is lower risk since the provider infrastructure is solid; the remaining work is the prompt engineering and UI rendering.

plan_updates: Updated plan to reflect current implementation state (99/100, 470+ tests), identified 6 unimplemented core features, and surfaced decisions on phasing, canvas library, voice capture, offline sync timing, and agent chat integration approach.
